clinicalPearls: Perineural (Tarlov) cysts are cerebrospinal-fluid-filled dilatations of the nerve-root sheath, most commonly at the sacral (S2/S3) levels
The majority are incidental and asymptomatic, found on MRI performed for other reasons
When symptomatic they can cause sacral or perineal pain, radiculopathy, and sometimes bladder, bowel, or sexual dysfunction
Symptoms may be positional, worsening with standing, the Valsalva manoeuvre, or activities that raise cerebrospinal fluid pressure
They are distinguished from other meningeal cysts by containing nerve-root fibres within the cyst wall or cavity
MRI shows a well-defined cystic lesion following cerebrospinal fluid signal, often with bony scalloping of the sacrum
Because incidental cysts are common, symptoms must be carefully correlated before attributing them to the cyst
Most are managed conservatively, and selected symptomatic cysts may be treated with image-guided aspiration or surgical fenestration and imbrication, although recurrence is a recognised problem
reference.pathophysiology: Tarlov (perineural) cysts are dilatations of the meningeal sheath around the posterior nerve root and dorsal root ganglion, most often in the sacral region. They contain cerebrospinal fluid and, characteristically, nerve-root fibres within their wall or lumen. A ball-valve mechanism is proposed, whereby cerebrospinal fluid enters the cyst but leaves less readily, allowing gradual enlargement, and raised cerebrospinal fluid pressure such as during the Valsalva manoeuvre may drive expansion. Progressive growth can compress adjacent nerve roots and erode the surrounding bone, producing radicular or sphincter symptoms in the minority who become symptomatic.
additionalDifferentials: Lumbosacral disc herniation or stenosis with radiculopathy
Sacral tumour such as chordoma or schwannoma, or an anterior sacral meningocele
Endometriosis for cyclical perineal or pelvic symptoms
Pelvic floor or gynaecological and urological pathology
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the lumbosacral spine and sacrum, following cerebrospinal fluid signal and showing nerve-root fibres
CT or CT myelography to assess bony scalloping and any communication with the thecal sac
Careful clinical correlation of symptoms with the cyst location and level
Urodynamic studies if bladder dysfunction is present
Imaging to exclude alternative sacral pathology
redFlags: New or progressive bladder, bowel, or sexual dysfunction
Features suggesting a solid sacral tumour rather than a simple cyst
reference.prognosis: Most perineural cysts are asymptomatic and require only reassurance; symptomatic cysts have a more variable course, and although intervention can relieve symptoms in selected patients, recurrence and cerebrospinal-fluid-related complications temper outcomes.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to an incidental cyst without careful correlation
Overlooking an alternative, treatable cause of sacral radicular symptoms
Underestimating the risk of cerebrospinal fluid leak and recurrence after intervention
management: Reassure and observe the majority, which are incidental and asymptomatic, without intervention
Manage symptomatic cysts conservatively with analgesia, neuropathic pain agents, physiotherapy and avoidance of activities that raise cerebrospinal fluid pressure
Consider image-guided percutaneous aspiration, often with fibrin glue injection, for selected symptomatic cysts
Reserve surgical options such as cyst fenestration, imbrication or wrapping for refractory cases, accepting a risk of recurrence and cerebrospinal-fluid complications
Assess and manage bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction, with urodynamic studies where indicated
Escalate urgently for progressive neurological deficit or new sphincter disturbance
Refer symptomatic or enlarging cysts to spinal neurosurgery
